implementation_notes: On the JVM Kotlin uses the same JPA mapping as Java: an @Embeddable child collected in @ElementCollection/@CollectionTable is loaded, inserted and deleted by the parent's persistence context, with no DAO for the child. Kotlin adds one caveat: Hibernate entities cannot be data classes (they need a no-argument constructor and identity-based equals/hashCode), so the child embeddable is a plain class with value-based equals/hashCode. Choose this when the service already runs a JPA container; the replacement semantics are the provider's, not yours.
pitfalls: Kotlin data classes cannot serve as JPA entities or embeddables without workarounds - use a plain class with explicit equals/hashCode or the provider's proxies and dirty checking misbehave.
Entity collections must stay mutable and field-accessed; a read-only List or a generated setter fights the persistence provider.

variants.name: Exposed DSL repository (hand-written)
variants.implementation_notes: JetBrains Exposed has no change tracking that would own the children, so the repository writes the parent and then deletes and batch-inserts the dependent rows inside a single transaction {}, which is the manual form of the pattern: the parent's mapper still owns the children and the child table has no DAO of its own. It suits Kotlin codebases that reject JPA's proxies and lazy loading, at the price of keeping the replacement semantics correct by hand.
pitfalls: The whole delete/insert must stay inside the transaction block; a query issued outside it silently drops the atomicity guarantee.
Exposed's DSL has no identity map, so loading the same order twice yields two independent object graphs - keep the repository the only entry point.
